title: Daily review
hookLine: a night account of the day
tomorrow: last shift of break. Dadi asks: what are you keeping from these weeks?

cards: Apps love a recap: your year in songs, your month in steps. Amira tried an older kind last night. Two columns in her notes app: what went well today, what went wrong.

The second column won by a mile. She typed one more line, "great, so I'm a mess," and went to bed feeling worse than before she started. So, the question for today: why look back at a day at all, if the list just hurts?

teach.b: Islam calls it muhasaba, taking account. In a report in al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet ﷺ says the wise person is the one who takes account of themselves and works for what comes after.
The caliph Umar is remembered for a line on it: take account of yourselves before you are taken to account. But the account isn't meant to end in "I'm a mess."

teach.h: A BAD DEED, THEN A GOOD ONE.
teach.b: In another report in al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet says: follow a bad deed with a good one, and it will wipe it out. So the night list isn't a verdict.
It's a to-do list for tomorrow, kept before a God the Qur'an calls forgiving and merciful, over and over. Now a neighbor.
In the Buddhist scriptures, the Buddha asks his young son Rahula: what is a mirror for? For looking at yourself, Rahula answers.

teach.h: BEFORE GOD, OR BEFORE THE MIRROR.
teach.b: Then do the same with your actions, the Buddha says: before, during and after, ask whether this led to harm for me, for others, or both. If it did, admit it and hold back next time.
If it didn't, be glad, and keep training day and night.
Two traditions, the same nightly look in the mirror. And one honest difference: for a Muslim, the account is kept before God, who forgives and will one day take account.
In the Buddha's teaching to Rahula, the question is harm and its causes, with no judge on a throne.

how: Muslims who practice muhasaba often take a few minutes before sleep, after 'Isha, to look back at the day, ask God's forgiveness for wrongs and thank Him for the good; some keep a small notebook for it.

o: a night account of the day, kept before God, both columns
a list of goals written at sunrise for the coming day
a weekly confession of sins said aloud to an imam

games.q: two mirrors at night — tap the pairs.
p: followed by a good one, wiped out
take account before you're taken to account
a mirror is for looking at yourself

s: a hadith says to follow a bad deed with a good one, which wipes it out
in al-Tirmidhi. the night list is a to-do list for tomorrow, not a verdict.
the point of muhasaba is to feel as bad as possible about the day
it's an account kept before a forgiving God, so tomorrow can be better; the good is counted too.
the Buddha's mirror teaching and muhasaba are the same practice under two names
they share the nightly look back; muhasaba is before God who forgives, while Rahula's mirror asks about harm, with no judge.

games.q: a friend from a Buddhist family says she does a nightly reflection 'like a mirror.' she asks if it's the same as your muhasaba. what's honest?
o: the same thing exactly; all religions teach one practice.
not alike at all; hers isn't really a religious practice.
a shared habit of looking back, with a real difference: for me, it's before God.
games.why: Rahula's mirror and muhasaba share the nightly look at your own actions. the difference is honest and nobody ranks: before God who forgives, or a question about harm and its causes.

practice: Count back through today, from now to waking. Name three things that went well, however small, one finger for each. Then name one thing to follow with something better tomorrow, and let the counting stop there.

wordCard.voice: Daily review: muhasaba, a night account of the day, kept before God, where each wrong is followed by a good and the good is counted too.

orig.note: Arabic: taking account, reckoning with oneself.

carryVoice: Before the light goes off: count the day, both columns, and close it. Thirteen of fourteen.

sources.ref: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2459 (the wise one takes account of himself; with Umar's saying, 'take account of yourselves before you are taken to account')
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1987 (follow a bad deed with a good one and it will wipe it out)
Majjhima Nikaya 61, Ambalatthika-rahulovada Sutta (the Buddha's mirror teaching to Rahula)
